newsitem.title: UK: Britain alleged lax in Chernobyl aftermath checks.
newsitem.headline: Britain alleged lax in Chernobyl aftermath checks.

text.p: Britain may have been lax in testing food after the Chernobyl nuclear disaster and exposed its citizens to an increased risk of cancer, a former government scientist was quoted on Thursday as saying.

John Jeffers, former director of the Institute of Terrestrial Ecology, told New Scientist magazine that monitoring of radiation in food such as milk after the accident in Ukraine in April, 1986, was "half-hearted and fairly ridiculous".
Jeffers added that no systematic efforts were made to trace where food had become contaminated after the world's worst nuclear accident.
He said that in the immediate aftermath of the accident there was no government funding into the behaviour of radioactivity in moorlands.
"We could have learned a great deal about how radionuclides moved through different ecosystems but we fluffed it," he was quoted as saying.
Britain's Ministry of Agrioculture defended its record against the allegations, saying that in 1986 it tested 28,490 samples of milk, vegetables, fruit, cereals and sheep for radiation.
Iodine levels in milk reached only a fifth of safety limits recommended by the government's National Radiological Protection Broad, the ministry said.
